en: [Page 67] [A Collection of Well-Spoken Verses] [Homage to Sarasvatī]

In the month of spring, the *laṅkā* (mango) trees, having attained their splendor through their leaves and shoots, dispelled the cold and subsequently became covered in *kali* fruits. Having raised her finger under the pretext of a *kali* fruit, she greatly increased the pride of the *mālatī* creeper. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 1)
The *mādhavī* creeper wards off the young bee coming toward me with her hands of wind-tossed shoots;
she says: "Defiled by my association with the jasmine, the queen of flowers, do not touch me. (Subhāṣitaratnakośasaṃgraha 2–3)
"The *mālatī* creeper, the temple of the god of love, blooming very slowly—she has been enjoyed by that clever six-legged bee in such a way that she does not tremble.
The beggars wash their feet with the talk of the fragrance [of the lotuses], which is superior to all other trees.
(Subhāṣitāvalī 5) Even those standing nearby are not seen as miserable by the wealthy, whose eyes are filled with the pollen from the blossoms of Lakṣmī’s lotus-hands. (Subhāṣitāvalī 6)
The swans of the mind are captivated by the mere sight of her, whose river-like limbs are tawny with the pollen of golden *kaṇṇikāra* flowers scattered by the sun’s rays.
Surely, Lakṣmī has been defiled by contact with the poison of the wicked Kālakūṭa. (*Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha* 7)

Those men who were seen by her instantly have their eyes closed [in death]. (Subhāṣitāvalī 8) What contradiction can there be regarding the power of wealth to snatch away the hearing and sight of men?
That it does not cause death—even though it is a sibling to poison—is truly a marvel. (Subhāṣitāvalī 9)
Even while seeing, they do not see; even while knowing, they do not know;
even while hearing, they truly do not hear, having become attached to sovereignty.
Even those who are not kings become kings; even those who are kings go as those who are departing.

O! May that Lakṣmī be victorious, together with whom all the hosts of virtues dwell! (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 11) At the time of lovemaking, necklaces are removed by women from the circle of their breasts;
even those possessing merit are set aside at a distance when they lack an occasion. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 12)
O Palāśa tree, the birds have long since abandoned all hope for your fruit;
for when your blossoms first appeared, they made their faces dark with grief. (Subhāṣitāvalī 13)
O Mother! Having swallowed bitter words and having tasted the pungent [poison] from the Kṣatriyas as well as from the clouds, even the abundant water given by them was enough for him;
for even the Moon, having honored the great ocean, lies upon its lap. (Subhāṣitāvalī 14)

Whether that is indeed contrary to worldly custom, or rather it appears fitting for those who are capable—[it is better] that those devoid of merit should be satisfied with the acquisition of even a small amount;
for the virtuous, by failing to obtain fruit corresponding to their virtues, merely suffer. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 15–16)
That the Lord of Night steals away the splendor of the moon-lotus groves even from within [the heart] is not fitting for him; or rather, what shame is there in one who bears a stain?
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 17) There will be no doubt that the Lord of the Gods will become powerful when Murāri is pleased.
Bound and fallen into the netherworld, this sound will not cease. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 18) Even the false attribution of a quality can arise in one who has manifested manly effort;
even for a lion in a solitary forest, the reputation of being "five-faced" is born. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 19)
That sound, that whiteness, and even that very birth from the lotus—
all these have been completely defiled by the crookedness of the conch’s heart. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 20) A necklace for the chest, earrings for the ears, and a girdle for the hips.
Even on a great festival, collyrium-sticks are for the eyes alone.
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 21) Whatever vessel is the receptacle for a certain amount of wealth, it receives only that much;
even when a rain-cloud pours down, water does not remain upon a mountain. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 22)
One who is devoid of merit cannot enjoy prosperity even if he has attained it; like a thirsty dog that licks up abundant water with its tongue, [he fails to partake of it]. Subhāṣitasamgraha 23.
O fortunate one, your pride dissolves when [the truth] is very near; what fault is there in you?

Even though she is gazing [at him], she does not see him; the kohl-stick is still clinging [to her eye]. (Subhāṣitasaṃdoha 24) In their proper places, virtues become manifest; places are made manifest by virtues.
Kohl beautifies the eyes, and the eyes beautify the kohl. (Subhāṣitasaṃdoha 25)
The power of collyrium resting upon the eyes of a most beautiful young woman is such that its virtues manifest themselves in various places;
so too is the splendor of a necklace resting upon the breasts of a most beautiful young woman. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 26)

Virtues do not expand as much in various positions as they do within the shell of a pearl-oyster. Even when its bamboo base is cut away, the Viñjha mountain does not abandon its support for the elephant. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 27)
The great, who bear the seal of their own reputation, protect what they have promised. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 28) Let the head be cut off, or let there be imprisonment; let fortune depart entirely.
For noble men, let whatever happens happen, provided that they protect what they have promised. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 29)
Great men abandon wealth, cast off their retinue, and even relinquish their own lives; they never, under any circumstances, allow a breach of their vow.
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 30) Let alone other people—even the five elements that constitute one's own body [are abandoned].

It is those very people who feel shame when they abandon what has been undertaken. (Subhāṣitasamgraha 31) For noble persons, the binding of speech is a greater protection than strong iron chains or various other bonds of snares. (Subhāṣitasamgraha 32)

In the flush of youth, actions are undertaken without reflection; when one reaches the decline of age, those very same deeds cause the heart to ache. But those insights which blossom through the mature contemplation of one's past actions—*Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha* 33.

If those [desires] are present at the very first beginning, why is that not sufficient? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 34) At the very outset, whatever desire arises under the influence of anger should not be acted upon; for if it is indeed carried out, its consequence will not be auspicious. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 35)

The virtuous do not praise that which has been accomplished without first examining what must be done; yet, even if it subsequently falls apart after being thoroughly examined, it does not produce blame.
For the noble-born, death itself is preferable to blame in the midst of one's kinsmen. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 36)

Furthermore, that death which occurs is the transformation of time common to the world. (Subhāṣita-saṃgraha 37) O Kṛṣṇa! How small is this earth compared to you who are so mighty? For one seeking [you], not only am I insignificant, but even I have been rendered light [insignificant]. (Subhāṣita-saṃgraha 38)
"O Kṛṣṇa, why do you, filled with indignation, reproach me when you yourself are at fault here? By whom was this small earth created?
"O Mother, do not give birth to such a son who is intent on begging from others! (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 39)

Even though you have approached her, do not hold onto that [hope], for she has caused the frustration of your request. (Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 40) "Why were you born so wretched? Why did you not perish even while dwelling in the womb?
For women, lack of wealth is an ornament, but it is not so for men. (Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 41)
Know that the self alone is difficult to conquer; what is the use of those [sons] born?
Even by those who are very capable, but do not benefit others, nothing at all is achieved. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 42)
A favor is done for the wicked person that very moment;
however, the good person bears the suffering with a great weight of kindness. (Subhāṣita-saṃgraha 43) May the earth support two types of men, or rather, may the earth be supported by both.
"He whose mind is set on doing good, who does not forget a favor received" (Subhāṣita-saṃgraha 44).
"If an elephant has been mocked by a pack of dogs in the middle of the marketplace upon being seen, is it fitting for that elephant to engage in a quarrel with the dogs? (Subhāṣita-saṃgraha 45).
Even a good person must endure a wicked one, even if capable of retorting;
for the body does not take away the glory of the bull while it remains hidden behind its back.
(Subhāṣitāvalī 46) The wind uproots and carries away trees only after knowing that their roots are shallow.
Great trees grow great roots; the great produce great growth.
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 47) If the great do not indeed perform a great service for the great, who else would reproach them?
Who would blame the Vindhya mountain for being moistened by the clouds? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 48)
The ill-fortuned grow angry at those of good fortune; poverty grows angry at wealthy people;
fools grow angry at wise men; and unchaste women grow angry at chaste ones.
This one [the moon], appearing as if made of nectar, is the sole delighter of the eyes and the mind.
This one has a body made of clear crystal, yet this other is difficult to endure.
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 50) A mouth is said to be "red" only when it is dear to someone; what is the use of further explanation?
The courtyard itself proclaims the prosperity within the house. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 51)
People consider these eyes to be the very essence of their lives;
they bloom when the beloved is seen, alas! yet they close in his absence.
Even love that is overflowing with passion is shattered into a thousand pieces by jealous pride. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 52)
Like salt scorched by the fire of the sun, [it is consumed] with a crackling sound;
O beloved! Even though they are well-savored with the essence of affection and passion, loves in time fade away like handfuls of water, through the mere absence of sight. (Subhāṣitasaṃdoha 53–54)
When the heart is overwhelmed by passion, when affection has dissolved and all sincerity has vanished,
what kind of love can there be in such a request? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 55)
O lotus-eyed one! While others enter another's body only after their life has departed, you, however, mount a body that is still living and whose form remains unimpaired.
O handsome one! Where did you learn this skill, so worthy of entering another's city? *Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha* 56.
By whom was she first established in my heart at our very first meeting? Subhāṣitāvalī 57.
If that treasure-house of beauty has been seen by your eyes, then let those limbs of yours roll about;
why do they wither away when they have not attained union? Subhāṣitāvalī 58.

Having seen the young woman... with their rolling eyes like those of a carpenter, even the lamp, its mind fixed on her, does not know the oil has run out. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṅgraha 59) This one wanders about, O friend—he who [steals] the hearts of women...
By that very sight, she makes a cleverly fashioned girdle for her hips.
(Subhāṣitāvalī 60) Some woman, O friend, makes [her bower] resound with the cries of pigeons, the warbling of cuckoos, and the cooing of doves!
When there is a lover who is so fond of pleasure, whence can there be pain? (Subhāṣitāvalī 61)
The young women, with their long locks of hair, earrings, and dangling strings of pearls, look beautiful like Vidyādharīs on a mountain peak;
for the water that falls as he plays with the boys is delightful. (Subhāṣitāvalī 62)

It refreshes the limbs of her beloved, which have been scorched by the fire of separation from her teacher. (Subhāṣitāvalī 63) In that lake where young women with heated limbs bathe, tortoises appear there as if they were made of glowing embers. (Subhāṣitāvalī 64)
"Alas! I do not know the field; let the rice be devoured by the flocks of parrots.
Even though they know, those wretched travelers ask me the way.
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 65) "How can that poor, sweet-voiced female sparrow protect [the grain], when her movement and gait are so slow?"
The drum does not keep time with her full, uplifted, and heavy breasts. (Subhāṣitāvalī 66) When the beloved guest has arrived, what can even a swift messenger do?
A wretched blind man remains blind even when his eyes are rubbed with ointment. (Subhāṣitāvalī 67)

Even between the virtuous who have attained prosperity and the wealthy who possess great virtues, there is indeed no mutual disparagement, just as there is none between mountains by their roots and their peaks.
Even if one wanders in the Nandana grove, enchanting with its swaying *kaṅkelli* sprouts... [Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 68]
Nevertheless, the playful movements of Maru’s hips cause a throbbing in Karaha’s heart. Subhāṣitāvalī 69 [p.
The dark and radiant braid-staff shines upon the orb of her buttocks.
O beautiful one! Like a serpent guarding the great treasure of wine, [how can sorrow be appeased]?
How can suffering be extinguished in that heart which is already tormented by pain?
For the suffering of this world does not transfer [to another], just as a reflection does not pass into a mirror. (Subhāṣitāvalī 70–71)
If there is loss for those who are overwhelmed by the blows of combat, let it be; what fault is there?
But that one should flee, abandoning the sky [the battlefield], is not fitting for heroes.
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 72) One who has been struck flees with his back turned, having abandoned the firmament.
Nevertheless, he is still called "the Sun"; behold the power of renown!

(Subhāṣitāvalī 73) Even though being eclipsed, the Moon endures the humiliation until the full moon; but when the Sun sets after robbing it of its splendor, it cannot endure the fragmentation. (Subhāṣitāvalī 74)
O Moon! endure day after day the pains of wandering through the courtyard of the sky and being eclipsed;
for it is not with ease that one makes oneself famous throughout the world. (Subhāṣitāvalī 75) Only that is a true birth in which the fruit is rich with a fragrant scent.

This [beauty] exists only in the flower; indeed, it perishes in the fruit. (Subhāṣitāvalī 76) The splendor produced by even a single swan standing on the bank of a shore is not attained by a multitude of flocks of cranes, however numerous. (Subhāṣitāvalī 77)
Just as a swan displays its graceful flight-path over the blossoming lotuses of Lake Mānasa, does a wretched crow even know how to lift its foot?
Just as the sweet warbling of a peacock with its plumage spread out is beautiful... [Subhāṣitāvalī 78]
Likewise, what can be done by a crow wandering even for a day in the forest?
(Subhāṣitasaṃdoha 79) It soars through the path of the sky, it casts off its dark color, and it displays itself as such;
yet a dung-heap calf cannot attain the conduct of a bee. (Subhāṣitasaṃdoha 80)

Love, which was dulled by the very presence of the happiness derived from the continuous play of unrestrained passion, becomes fresh once more when sharpened on the whetstone of jealous anger. O handsome one, where did you learn this state of supreme sweetness that arises after lovemaking? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 81) O handsome one, where did you learn this state of supreme sweetness that arises after lovemaking? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 81) O handsome one, where did you learn this state of supreme sweetness that arises after lovemaking
"Whether it be through association with dogs, or whether it be because of your association, O dog—look at the tracks of the feet of these excellent women during their dalliance!
It is evident that a prop was provided for the one falling upon his own excrement. (Subhāṣitāvalī 82–83)
Whatever artful dalliance is performed by couples during their union with the god of love, remembering which at the conclusion they become mutually ashamed. (Subhāṣitāvalī 84)
Thus they embraced one another, their limbs weakened by separation, as if they had become a single entity through the fire of the heated arrows of love;
struck by the blows of incessantly falling torrents of water, they languish. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 85)

"Those whose elephants have been burnt do not find a dwelling because of their great height. (Subhāṣitāvalī 86) "Just as you, O Vindhya, embrace the female deer, so too, if the lord of the deer were alone, the Pulindas would not deprive him of his sovereignty while he was alive. (Subhāṣitāvalī 87)

O Rāhu! If you, who once bore the moon—the abode of the deer—could have endured the lion’s roar, then it would have been difficult for you to humble [Indra’s] pride. O Pālitaka! Tell me clearly: while wandering over the entire circle of the earth, [have you ever seen such a thing]? *Subhāṣitāvalī* 88.
Where has fire ever been seen or heard of as cool as sandalwood juice?
For a man of pure conduct who is tormented by the oppression of injustice, it is clear that even fire becomes cool like sandalwood juice. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 89–90)
A good person of pure nature becomes even more stainless when rubbed by wicked folk,
just as a mirror becomes cleaner when wiped with ash.
(Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 91) Why should a sword be used for what can be cut by a lotus leaf?
When something sweet ought to be said, what is the use of speaking something bitter?
Follow [the right path], speak what is pleasant, and keep the task in mind with your heart.
The peacock speaks sweetly, yet it eats the venomous serpent. (Subhāṣitasamgraha 92–93)

Know with your heart that whatever action is as sweet as the speech of a *jambu* flower is like a peacock: it speaks sweetly, yet it eats a venomous serpent. (Subhāṣita-saṃgraha 94) When a task has arisen, one accommodates even a wicked person of bad character.

"Why is neem not drunk for the sake of protecting the body? [One might ask. "He who cannot be endured without being appeased—even when he has committed an offense—is beloved by whom, tell me, during a city fire, even though he is on the ground? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 95–96)
Even in this identical human birth, the wicked man burns, while the virtuous man brings delight;
armor alone protects life, whereas the sword takes it away. Even under the same heat of fire, golden leaves kiss the boil. *Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 97*
The anklet on the Śyāmā’s foot slips down onto her thigh;
a man accomplishes great deeds indeed—of this there is no doubt. (Subhāṣitāvalī 98) [p. 74]

Like the dust of a rose-scented tunnel, he indeed does not become manifest. (Subhāṣitāvalī 99) How do those who have not established themselves in a state worthy of praise by the virtuous not feel ashamed, even though they boast of the greatness of their ancestors? (Subhāṣitāvalī 100)
"O friend with unblinking eyes! Because I have drunk the beauty of my beloved, my limbs are today being massaged with ointment, dear friend!
O large-eyed one! He is blessed for whose sake [my heart] is choked with emotion. (Subhāṣitāvalī 101)
Sighs depart pregnant with the rising of the fifth arrow [of love].

(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 102) Blessed are those who, at the time when love-play has begun by others who have come for food, cause their high and beautiful breasts to throb against the hearts [of their lovers]. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 103)
Speaking thus with his body undivided, he said: "O beautiful one!

Today it has been proven, O lovely one with teeth and nails worn down! Indeed, my heart is breaking within you. Why do you embrace me while breathing hot sighs and turning away from me? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 104)
Having first scorched my heart, you now set my back ablaze.
(Subhāṣitāvalī 105) Being led away by various young women who are themselves enslaved by their own karma, this very tree of medicinal herbs does not shed its bark from its limbs. (Subhāṣitāvalī 106)
Even in a difficult undertaking, the steadfast man does not abandon the commencement of his task;
prosperity falls upon his chest like a pursuing woman. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 107) For she was not spoken to by people as she climbed along the path of the street, being afraid.
That very same fever of separation still throbs within my heart even today.
(Subhāṣitāvalī 108) One who is pierced by your eye-arrows lives happily, while one who is not pierced dies; by whom was this unprecedented science of archery taught? (Subhāṣitāvalī 109)
Even when dead, it burns the body, like powdered conch-shell;
so what can I do, O Mother, against this one whose passion has been conquered? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 110) They speak with words that are somehow dear, even though they are devoid of true affection.
Just as they are regarded as kinsmen by the world, the wise are carried on the head;
even though he is joined with the ocean’s poison, the moon dwells upon the head of Śiva.
Wherever the wise go, there they are carried on the head. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 111–112)
A position is obtained through virtues; therefore, one must certainly cultivate the appreciation of virtues.
Even a necklace, if devoid of gems, cannot rest upon the surface of a young woman’s breast. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 113)
Clouds do not rain after merely thundering; lords do not give after merely smiling; and trees that have blossomed do not bear fruit—how can they not feel ashamed?
(Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 114) Having the nectar of immortality at his own disposal, yet failing to create a world of immortal bodies...

O Lord of Rivers, you do not feel shame before your exultant waves! (Subhāṣitāvalī 115) For beings who have gone abroad, become intoxicated by passion, and are tormented by grief, even the sight of their own dog returning from its own country brings happiness. (Subhāṣitāvalī 116)
There is another, some seventh rasa, which brings about the bliss of all limbs, and which is imagined to be superior to the first union with a beloved;
that which is not heard of in the treatises and which remains beyond the reach even of the great poets. (Subhāṣitāvalī 117)
In the first union with a new lover, whatever it may be, the beloved gives that very pleasure.
(Subhāṣitāvalī 118) Whichever one pleases is the salty one; O Brahmin, what need is there to say more?
Having abandoned the taste of sugar-candy pills, one finds satisfaction even in clay. (Subhāṣitāvalī 119)

Just as there is no secret that does not exist, O beloved! let the form become like a great ocean; let the taste of even the most dreadful things become sweet through patience. (Subhāṣitasaṃgraha 120, Dohā) Those things which are bitter at the beginning become like the essence of nectar in their final transformation.

Those actions which are well-considered do not cause people to laugh. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 121) You speak like a lotus stalk, yet in your heart you are as crooked as a deer's horn; through your assumed straightforwardness, you are worthy of praise by others. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 122)
"Since you have little affection for him, he too has little affection for you, my daughter!
O long-eyed one, a palm tree is certainly not struck by a single hand. "O Śyāmā, where the lion goes, there he goes; it is not fitting for him to stay upon a mere leaf. *Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha* 123.

A true person is exactly like that; touch my eyes—what is the use of weeping? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 124) Even having acquired knowledge, even having performed courageous deeds, and even having leaped over Mount Meru, where is there happiness without merits? (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 125)
Speech uttered at the proper time is beautiful; speech uttered at the proper time brings happiness;
but speech uttered out of season destroys even that which has been accomplished. (Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 126) Just as both hands of a mouse are occupied with a single grain of rice.
Likewise, those who do not recognize excellence become arrogant even over a trifle.
Virtues become manifest and highly prized only among people who know how to appreciate them; even jewels and gems [are so valued] because of the cowherd... [Subhāṣitagāthāsaṃgraha 127–128].
